content: House dust mites are a significant source of allergens found in household dust, and these allergens are known to exacerbate asthma symptoms in individuals who are sensitive to them. Various strategies, including chemical, physical, and combined approaches, have been developed to reduce the levels of these allergens in the home environment with the aim of alleviating asthma symptoms. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions designed to reduce exposure to house dust mite allergens in the homes of individuals with asthma who are sensitive to these allergens. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in PubMed and the Cochrane Airways Group Register, with the last search performed in July 2011. No restrictions were applied regarding the language of the studies. The review included randomized controlled trials that compared house dust mite control measures to placebo or no treatment in individuals with confirmed sensitivity to house dust mites. Two reviewers independently applied the inclusion criteria, assessed the quality of the studies, and extracted data. Where necessary, the authors of the trials were contacted to clarify or provide additional information. A total of 55 trials involving 3,121 participants were included in the analysis. Of these, 37 trials investigated physical methods of allergen reduction, with 26 specifically using mattress encasings. Ten trials evaluated chemical methods, and eight trials assessed a combination of chemical and physical approaches. Despite the inclusion of a large number of studies, many were of poor methodological quality, which could have led to an overestimation of the reported effects. The primary outcome assessed was morning peak expiratory flow, which was reported in 1,665 participants. The standardized mean difference (SMD) for this outcome was 0.01, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) ranging from -0.08 to 0.11, indicating no significant effect. Similarly, there were no statistically significant differences in other outcomes, including the proportion of patients reporting improvement (risk ratio 1.01, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.27), asthma symptom scores (SMD -0.06, 95% CI -0.16 to 0.05), or medication usage (SMD -0.05, 95% CI -0.17 to 0.07). Based on these findings, the authors concluded that neither chemical nor physical methods for reducing exposure to house dust mite allergens can be recommended as effective interventions for managing asthma in mite-sensitive individuals. Furthermore, the authors expressed skepticism regarding the value of conducting additional studies similar to those included in this review. If future research is pursued, it should employ rigorous methodologies, explore alternative approaches, and ensure careful monitoring of both mite exposure and clinically relevant outcomes.
